draft.title: Criteria for typical behaviour
card: Psychologists judge whether behaviour is typical by testing it against criteria. No single criterion is used alone.
is the behaviour accepted in the person's own culture? Social norm: does it follow the unwritten rules of a group or society?
is the behaviour uncommon, far from the average in the population? Personal distress: does it cause the person ongoing suffering?
does the behaviour get in the way of daily life, such as study, work, relationships or self-care?
draft.remember: Typical behaviour is judged by culture, norms, rarity, distress and how well the person can function.

a.q: Hana avoids school, work and friends because she feels constant fear. Her fear stops her from caring for herself. Which criterion does this show most directly?
opts: The behaviour breaks a social norm
a.why: Her behaviour interferes with daily life and self-care, so it is maladaptive. Rarity is tempting, but the case says nothing about how common her fear is.
a.clue: Think about what her fear stops her doing.

b.q: Tom lives in a small town in Victoria. He sings loudly on a quiet train, and other passengers look uncomfortable. Which criterion is being used to judge his behaviour?
opts: Social norms about behaviour in public
Maladaptive effect on Tom's daily life
b.why: The passengers are reacting to an unwritten rule about how to act on a quiet train, so the social norm criterion applies. Nothing suggests Tom is distressed or that singing stops him functioning, so those criteria do not fit.
b.clue: Who is reacting, and to what kind of rule?

b.best: Social norms about behaviour in public

proposal.title: Criteria for typical behaviour
card: Psychologists judge whether behaviour is typical by testing it against criteria, which are standards for comparison. Cultural perspective asks: is the behaviour accepted within the person's own culture?
Social norms ask: does the behaviour follow the unwritten rules of a group or society about how to act in a setting?
Statistical rarity asks: is the behaviour uncommon, far from the average in the population? Personal distress asks: does it cause the person ongoing suffering or upset?
The maladaptive criterion asks: does the behaviour get in the way of daily life, such as study, work, relationships or self-care?
proposal.remember: Typical behaviour is judged by culture, norms, rarity, distress and how well the person can function.

a.q: Hana avoids school, work and friends because she feels constant fear. Her fear stops her from caring for herself. Which criterion does this show most directly?
opts: The behaviour breaks a social norm
a.why: Her behaviour interferes with study, relationships and self-care, so it is maladaptive. Rarity is tempting, but the case says nothing about how common her fear is in the population.
a.clue: Think about what her fear stops her doing.

b.q: Tom sings loudly on a quiet train. Other passengers frown, because people are expected to keep quiet there. Which criterion are they using to judge him?
opts: Social norms about behaviour in public
Maladaptive effect on Tom's daily life
b.why: The passengers are reacting to an unwritten rule about how to act on a quiet train, so the social norm criterion applies. Rarity is tempting, but they are judging him against an expectation, not against how common singing is.
b.clue: What are the passengers comparing his behaviour with?
